warmup.q: A topic has one partition. Three consumers join one consumer group, and three other consumers join one share group. How many members of each group receive records?
options: 1 in the consumer group, 1 in the share group
1 in the consumer group, 3 in the share group
3 in the consumer group, 1 in the share group
warmup.why: A consumer group gives each partition to exactly one member, so two members sit idle (lesson 8). A share group's members all read the partition, and the broker hands each record to one of them under a lock. The Try-it shows it: one consumer-group member gets all 12 records, and the three share-group members get four each.

sections.h: A consumer group can't run more consumers than partitions
sections.html:
Lesson 1 of this track built a queue: the broker tracks every message, hands each one to one consumer and deletes it once it is acknowledged. Lesson 2 replaced it with a log that keeps everything and tracks one number per reader, and lessons 3 to 10 built on that. This lesson brings the queue back, on top of the log, and starts with the problem that made Kafka add it.

The notification service sends an SMS for every authorized payment, and each send takes about 200 ms because the SMS provider is slow. The notifications topic has 6 partitions, so the service's consumer group can use at most 6 consumers (lesson 8): one owner per partition, and a seventh consumer sits idle. Six consumers at 5 sends a second each make 30 a second. On a sale day payments reach 300 a second, and the backlog grows by 270 every second.

Each consumer-group fix hurts. More partitions: 60 of them for 60 consumers, chosen up front because adding partitions later moves keys (lesson 5), and nearly empty for most of the year. Threads inside each consumer: possible, but the bookmark is one offset per partition, and it can only move past a record when every record before it is done, so you end up tracking finished offsets by hand (lesson 7). And a record that keeps failing still blocks its partition (lesson 9).

What the notification service wants is lesson 1's queue. Any free worker takes the next message and acknowledges it when it's done, and a message whose worker died goes to someone else. Order doesn't matter: two texts for two payments can go out either way round.

A share group gives a topic those semantics. Its members don't own partitions: they all read from all of them, and the broker hands out records one by one, so several members read one partition at the same time and the partition count no longer caps the number of consumers. You use KafkaShareConsumer instead of KafkaConsumer: the same subscribe and poll, and no assignment, seek or offset of your own. The topic doesn't change. A consumer group and a share group can read it at the same time, each with its own progress.

Java
try (var consumer = new KafkaShareConsumer<String, String>(Map.of(
        "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092",
        "group.id", "notify",                               // a share group: no partitions of its own
        "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) {
    consumer.subscribe(List.of("notifications"));
    while (running) {
        for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)))
            sms.send(r.value());                            // implicit mode: the next poll accepts this batch
    }
}
Kotlin
KafkaShareConsumer<String, String>(mapOf(
    "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
    "group.id" to "notify",                                 // a share group: no partitions of its own
    "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java, "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
)).use { consumer ->
    consumer.subscribe(listOf("notifications"))
    while (running) {
        for (r in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)))
            sms.send(r.value())                             // implicit mode: the next poll accepts this batch
    }
}

Share groups came with KIP-932: early access in Kafka 4.0, a preview in 4.1, production-ready since 4.2, and Kafka 4.4 added a broker-side dead-letter queue, covered below. A cluster with fewer than three brokers must lower the share coordinator's state topic to one replica (share.coordinator.state.topic.replication.factor and share.coordinator.state.topic.min.isr set to 1), as the lab broker does. The Try-it runs both kinds of group on a topic with one partition.

steps: From the labs folder, start the broker if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait.

Run ShareGroupDemo (command below). It creates a topic with one partition, starts three members of a consumer group and three of a share group, waits until all six have joined, then writes 12 notifications. Each member takes 100 ms per record. It takes 20 to 40 seconds.

Each member takes 100 ms per record, as if it called an SMS provider. */ public class ShareGroupDemo { static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; static final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(true); public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long run = System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000; String topic = "notifications-" + run, consumerGroup = "notify-cg-" + run, shareGroup = "notify-sg-" + run; try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(topic, 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); // a share group reads its settings from group configs; Map<String, List<Long>> got = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); AtomicInteger cgCount = new AtomicInteger(), sgCount = new AtomicInteger(); List<Thread> members = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { String c = "c" + i, s = "s" + i; got.put(c, Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>())); got.put(s, Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>())); members.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> groupMember(topic, consumerGroup, c, got.get(c), cgCount))); members.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> shareMember(topic, shareGroup, s, got.get(s), sgCount))); } awaitMembers(admin, consumerGroup, shareGroup); try (var p = new KafkaProducer<>(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP), new StringSerializer(), new StringSerializer())) { for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) p.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, 0, "acct-" + i, "notify-" + i)).get(); } long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 60_000_000_000L; while ((cgCount.get() < 12 || sgCount.get() < 12) && System.nanoTime() < deadline) Thread.sleep(100); running.set(false); for (Thread t : members) t.join(); System.out.println("consumer group: c1 got " + got.get("c1") + ", c2 got " + got.get("c2") + ", c3 got " + got.get("c3")); System.out.println("share group: s1 got " + got.get("s1") + ", s2 got " + got.get("s2") + ", s3 got " + got.get("s3")); } } static void groupMember(String topic, String group, String name, List<Long> got, AtomicInteger total) { try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<>(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "group.id", group, "group.protocol", "consumer", "auto.offset.reset", "earliest", "client.id", name), new StringDeserializer(), new StringDeserializer())) { c.subscribe(List.of(topic)); while (running.get()) handle(c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)), got, total); } } static void shareMember(String topic, String group, String name, List<Long> got, AtomicInteger total) { try (var c = new KafkaShareConsumer<>(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "group.id", group, "client.id", name, "max.poll.records", 2, "share.acquire.mode", "record_limit"), new StringDeserializer(), new StringDeserializer())) { c.subscribe(List.of(topic)); while (running.get()) handle(c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)), got, total); // implicit mode: the next poll accepts } } static void handle(ConsumerRecords<String, String> records, List<Long> got, AtomicInteger total) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { sleep(100); // send the SMS got.add(r.offset()); total.incrementAndGet(); } } /** Waits until both groups have their three members, so that no member starts with a head start. */ static void awaitMembers(Admin admin, String consumerGroup, String shareGroup) throws Exception { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 60_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < deadline) { try { int cg = admin.describeConsumerGroups(List.of(consumerGroup)).all().get().get(consumerGroup).members().size(); int sg = admin.describeShareGroups(List.of(shareGroup)).all().get().get(shareGroup).members().size(); if (cg == 3 && sg == 3) return; } catch (Exception e) { // the groups don't exist yet } Thread.sleep(200); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

Which consumer-group member owns the partition, and how the share group splits the records, change from run to run. The shape doesn't: one consumer-group member does all the work, while the share group spreads the same partition over all three members, two records at a time (max.poll.records=2 with share.acquire.mode=record_limit). Each record went to exactly one share member.

sections.h: The broker locks each record, and the consumer acknowledges it
sections.html:
How can three consumers read one partition and never get the same record? The broker keeps a state per record. For each partition a share group reads, it tracks the in-flight records, starting at the share-partition start offset (SPSO); every record before the SPSO is finished. Each in-flight record is in one of four states:

  • available: waiting for a consumer;
  • acquired: handed to one consumer, under a lock that runs out after share.record.lock.duration.ms (30 s by default);
  • acknowledged: done;
  • archived: given up on, never delivered again.

A poll acquires available records for that consumer, and each acquisition adds one to the record's delivery count. The consumer then acknowledges each record with one of four types. ACCEPT means done. RELEASE gives the record back for another try, for a transient failure such as a timeout at the SMS provider. REJECT archives it, for a permanent failure such as an invalid phone number. RENEW (Kafka 4.2, KIP-1222) extends the lock for a slow record. If the consumer dies or freezes, nobody acknowledges, the lock runs out, and the record becomes available to anyone. No heartbeat timeout or rebalance is needed for that.

Java
// share.acknowledgement.mode=explicit: every record gets its own answer
for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) {
    try {
        sms.send(r.value());
        consumer.acknowledge(r, AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT);      // done
    } catch (ProviderTimeout e) {
        consumer.acknowledge(r, AcknowledgeType.RELEASE);     // transient: try again, maybe on another member
    } catch (InvalidPhoneNumber e) {
        consumer.acknowledge(r, AcknowledgeType.REJECT);      // permanent: archive it (and DLQ it, in 4.4)
    }
}
consumer.commitSync();                                         // send the acknowledgements to the broker
Kotlin
// share.acknowledgement.mode=explicit: every record gets its own answer
for (r in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) {
    val ack = try {
        sms.send(r.value())
        AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT                                 // done
    } catch (e: ProviderTimeout) {
        AcknowledgeType.RELEASE                                // transient: try again, maybe on another member
    } catch (e: InvalidPhoneNumber) {
        AcknowledgeType.REJECT                                 // permanent: archive it (and DLQ it, in 4.4)
    }
    consumer.acknowledge(r, ack)
}
consumer.commitSync()                                          // send the acknowledgements to the broker

That loop runs in explicit mode (share.acknowledgement.mode=explicit); in the default implicit mode, the next poll accepts the whole previous batch. A record can't bounce forever. Once its delivery count reaches share.delivery.count.limit (5 by default), the next release or expired lock archives it. Since Kafka 4.4 (KIP-1191, with the feature share.version at 2), the broker can also write an archived record to a dead-letter topic named by the group config errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name. It writes the record's origin and delivery count as headers, and the record itself only with errors.deadletterqueue.copy.record.enable=true. By default the topic's name must start with dlq., and the topic needs errors.deadletterqueue.group.enable=true. The feature is new, and Confluent warns it may still change in a minor release.

Share groups take most settings from group configs, set with kafka-configs.sh --entity-type groups or the Admin client, and the broker bounds them: the lock between 15 and 60 seconds, the delivery limit between 2 and 10. share.auto.offset.reset is latest by default, so a new group skips what's already in the topic.

What you give up is order. Records of one batch arrive in offset order, but members work in parallel and redeliveries come back later, so there's neither per-key nor per-partition order. Use share groups for independent work items, never for a ledger.

steps: Run RedeliveryDemo (command below). Consumer c1 releases offset 0 every time, rejects offset 3 and accepts the rest; then the demo reads the group's dead-letter topic. Predict how many times offset 0 is delivered.

} } static void lockExpiry(String topic, String group) { var c1 = shareConsumer(group, "c1", "max.poll.records", 2, "share.acquire.mode", "record_limit"); c1.subscribe(List.of(topic)); List<Long> held = new ArrayList<>(); try (var c2 = shareConsumer(group, "c2")) { c2.subscribe(List.of(topic)); int seen = 0; while (seen < 6) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : c2.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { c2.acknowledge(r, AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT); sections.h: A share group is lesson 1's queue, rebuilt on a log
sections.html:
Put the three designs side by side and the share group's place is clear.

Queue (RabbitMQ 4.x quorum queue) Share group (Kafka 4.4) Consumer group (Kafka)
Progress is kept as a state per message a state per in-flight record one offset per partition
A consumer stops answering its messages return when its channel closes, or when a consumer timeout runs out each lock runs out after 30 s its partitions move after the session timeout or max.poll.interval.ms
Attempts before giving up 20 by default 5 by default no limit
Giving up means dropping, or a dead-letter exchange archiving, or the dlq. topic (4.4) whatever your code does (lesson 9)
After success the message is deleted the record stays in the log the record stays in the log
Order lost once there is redelivery and more than one consumer lost kept per partition

The top four rows say a share group is a queue: per-record state, a timer per delivery, a delivery limit and a place for the failures. The numbers differ and the ideas don't. RELEASE is a negative acknowledgement that puts a message back, REJECT is one that drops it, and the lock does the job of the queue's consumer timeout without waiting for a connection to close.

The fifth row is where it stays a log. A queue's acknowledgement is destructive: the broker deletes the message, so a second team that wants the same messages needs its own queue, filled from the start, and nobody can replay last week. A share group's ACCEPT changes only that group's state for the record. The record itself stays in the topic until retention, so a consumer group, a second share group or a replay next month can still read it, as lesson 2 promised. And the share group's state is small: records before the start offset are simply done, so the broker tracks only the in-flight window, by default at most 2,000 records per partition.

The two designs are growing toward each other from both sides. RabbitMQ streams are a log inside a queue broker, with reads that delete nothing, and share groups are a queue inside a log. When you choose, ask the questions from lesson 1 again: do the messages need an order, does anyone need to read them twice, and what should happen to one that keeps failing.

sections.h: Size partitions from measured rates, then watch lag
sections.html:
The partition count is the one number that's expensive to change (lesson 5, and the Partitioning track's lesson on rebalancing), so work it out. Measure two rates on your own hardware: how many records a second one partition takes from your producers, and how many one consumer instance processes. Divide your target by each, take the larger result, and leave room for growth.

An example. The ledger must handle 6,000 payments a second at peak two years from now. One partition takes 10,000 records a second from the producers, but one ledger consumer handles only 400 a second, because each payment is a database transaction. Producers need 1 partition; consumers need 15. Take 16, and key by account so that each account keeps its order.

More partitions aren't free. Each one is a set of segment and index files on every replica (lesson 3), a follower to keep in the ISR (lesson 4), a batch in every producer's memory (lesson 6), and a leader to elect when a broker fails. When the consumers are the limit and order doesn't matter, a share group is the cheaper fix.

Then watch consumer lag: for each partition, the log end offset minus the group's committed offset. Monitoring tools compute exactly that, with two admin calls, as the Try-it does. A lag in records means little on its own: 2,000 records is 5 seconds of work for a consumer that does 400 a second, and more than an hour for one that does 0.5. Alert on lag that keeps growing, or on the age of the oldest unprocessed record, not on a fixed count. And look per partition. A total of 2,000 can be two stuck partitions and one healthy one, which points at a poison pill (lesson 9) or a hot key (lesson 5). For a share group, kafka-share-groups.sh --describe shows, per partition, the start offset as the broker last recorded it and the lag: records not finished yet.

Old data costs disk. Tiered storage (KIP-405, production-ready since Kafka 3.9) copies closed segments to object storage such as S3 and keeps only the newest ones on the broker's disk. You turn it on per topic with remote.storage.enable=true; local.retention.ms decides how long segments stay local, and retention.ms still decides when data is gone. Brokers stay small and a new replica copies less, while a consumer that reads last month's payments makes the broker fetch them from the object store. Apache Kafka ships the framework but no production plugin for the object store, so you add one, and compacted topics can't use it.

A settlement group reads 1,000 of 3,000 payments in a 3-partition topic and commits. */ public class LagDemo { static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long run = System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000; } // what a lag exporter does: two admin calls, then a subtraction per partition Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> committed = admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets(group).partitionsToOffsetAndMetadata().get(); var ends = admin.listOffsets(committed.keySet().stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(tp -> tp, tp -> OffsetSpec.latest()))).all().get(); long total = 0; for (var e : new TreeMap<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata>((a, b) -> a.partition() - b.partition()) {{ putAll(committed); sections.h: Plain client, Spring Kafka or Quarkus, and a Flow for Kotlin
sections.html:
Every Kafka lesson in this track used the plain client, because the frameworks wrap it. Spring for Apache Kafka and Quarkus's messaging extension both run the poll loop and call your method per record. What they decide for you is what this track taught you to decide.

Plain client 4.4 Spring for Apache Kafka 4.1 Quarkus 3.40 messaging
Poll loop yours a listener container the Kafka connector
Commits yours (lesson 7) ack modes on the container commit strategies; throttled by default
Failures yours (lesson 9) error handlers, retry topics, dead letters failure strategies; fail by default, dead-letter-queue, delayed-retry-topic
Share groups KafkaShareConsumer ShareKafkaMessageListenerContainer check the guide for your version
Client it brings 4.4.0 kafka-clients 4.2.2 kafka-clients 4.1.1

The last row matters. A framework brings its own client version, so a feature newer than that client isn't there until the framework upgrades, whatever the brokers run. Brokers accept clients from 2.1 on, so the mix is safe. In one Gradle build, let each module use its framework's client version rather than forcing one.

In Kotlin you'd rather collect a Flow than write a while loop. Two facts from lesson 7 shape the wrapper. A consumer isn't thread-safe, so every call must come from one thread, and poll blocks that thread for up to its timeout. So the loop runs on one dedicated thread and hands records to the collector through the flow's channel, which also slows polling when the collector is slow. When the collector stops, the flow calls wakeup(), the one method another thread may call: a blocked poll throws WakeupException at once, and the poll thread closes the consumer. Commit on that thread too, never from the collector.

Java
Thread pollThread = new Thread(() -> {                       // every consumer call on this one thread
    try {
        while (true) for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(pollTimeout)) handoff.put(r);   // put waits for a slow worker
    } catch (WakeupException e) {
        // the worker is done and wakeup() ended a blocked poll
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    } finally {
        consumer.close();
    }
}, "kafka-poll");
pollThread.start();
// ... the worker takes records from handoff (an ArrayBlockingQueue) ...
consumer.wakeup();                                            // the one call another thread may make
pollThread.join();
Kotlin
fun <K, V> Consumer<K, V>.records(pollTimeout: Duration): Flow<ConsumerRecord<K, V>> = channelFlow {
    val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { Thread(it, "kafka-poll") }
    val consumer = this@records
    launch(executor.asCoroutineDispatcher()) {               // every consumer call on this one thread
        try {
            while (isActive) for (r in consumer.poll(pollTimeout)) send(r)   // send waits for a slow collector
        } catch (e: WakeupException) {
            // the collector is gone and wakeup() ended a blocked poll
        } finally {
            withContext(NonCancellable) { consumer.close() }
        }
    }.invokeOnCompletion { executor.shutdown() }
    awaitClose { consumer.wakeup() }                          // runs when the collector stops: another thread
}

The Java twin is the same design without coroutines: a poll thread, a small BlockingQueue and wakeup(). The lab builds the Kotlin one and tests it against a consumer whose poll blocks for 30 seconds.

refs.title: Spring for Apache Kafka: what's new in 4.1

analogy: A consumer group is a supermarket where each checkout lane owns its own queue of customers: fair and in order, but the number of lanes is fixed, and a slow customer holds up everyone behind them. A share group is the deli counter with numbered tickets: whichever server is free calls the next number, a ticket left unattended goes back on the board after 30 seconds, and after five failed attempts the ticket goes to the manager's desk (the dead-letter queue). The analogy breaks at the ticket roll: the share group's tickets are records in a log that stays there, so a consumer group can still read the same records in order at the same time.
world: Use share groups in your platform for work where each record stands alone: notifications, webhook deliveries to merchants, PDF statements, document checks that call a slow third party. Keep consumer groups for anything with an order or a running state: the ledger, balances, the payment state machine, anything a Temporal workflow reconstructs from events. Size the payments topic from the slowest consumer you must keep up with, key it by account, and alert on lag that keeps growing and on the age of the oldest record. Quarkus 3.40 bundles kafka-clients 4.1.1, from before share groups were production-ready in 4.2, so check its guide before you count on them there; a plain KafkaShareConsumer in its own module, or Spring Kafka 4.1's share container, works today. In Kotlin, wrap the poll loop in a Flow that owns one thread and calls wakeup() on cancellation, instead of calling poll from coroutines on a shared dispatcher.
mistake: Moving a consumer that needs order to a share group because it was slow. It scales at once, and then two events of one account arrive on two members at the same time: a refund is applied before its capture, or a statement is sent before the payment it lists. Share groups promise each record to one member, not order. Keep order-dependent work on a consumer group with enough partitions, keyed by the entity whose order matters, and move only independent work items to a share group. A second mistake, smaller: share.auto.offset.reset defaults to latest, so a new share group starts at the end and ignores the backlog that motivated it. Set it to earliest on the group before the first member joins.

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: // share.acknowledgement.mode=explicit: every record gets its own answer for (r in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { val ack = try { sms.send(r.value()) AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT // done } catch (e: ProviderTimeout) { AcknowledgeType.RELEASE // transient: try again, maybe on another member } catch (e: InvalidPhoneNumber) { AcknowledgeType.REJECT // permanent: archive it (and DLQ it, in 4.4) } consumer.acknowledge(r, ack) } consumer.commitSync() // send the acknowledgements to the broker

compare.note: The same three outcomes and one commitSync() per batch. Kotlin's try is an expression, so it computes the acknowledgement type and calls acknowledge once; Java calls it in each branch. In explicit mode every record of a batch must be acknowledged before the next poll, or the poll throws IllegalStateException. A RELEASE on the fifth delivery archives the record, so the code doesn't count attempts itself: the broker does.

The frozen consumer's acknowledgement is refused when it wakes up.

recap: A consumer group gives each partition to one member, so its parallelism stops at the partition count. A share group's members all read every partition, and the broker hands out records one by one (KIP-932, production-ready since 4.2).

Each in-flight record is available, acquired under a lock (30 s by default), acknowledged or archived. ACCEPT finishes it, RELEASE retries it, REJECT archives it, RENEW extends the lock; an expired lock frees it.
Every acquisition adds to the delivery count; at share.delivery.count.limit (5) the record is archived. Kafka 4.4 can write archived records to a dlq. topic, as headers by default.

Share groups are lesson 1's queue on a log: per-record state, locks and a delivery limit, but records stay in the log after they're done. They give up order, per key and per partition, so use them for independent work items and consumer groups for anything ordered or stateful.

Size partitions from measured rates: target divided by the per-partition producer rate and by the per-consumer rate, the larger of the two, plus growth. Watch lag per partition and its growth, not a fixed count.
Frameworks wrap the same loop and bring their own client version. In Kotlin, a Flow over one poll thread, with wakeup() on cancellation, keeps the consumer thread-confined.

explain.prompt: Your team's notification consumer can't keep up on sale days, and someone proposes going from 6 to 60 partitions. Explain the alternative, how it works, and when it would be the wrong choice.
explain.answer: A consumer group can't use more members than partitions, which is why they want 60. A share group removes that cap: all members read all partitions, and the broker hands out each record to one member under a lock, 30 seconds by default. Each member acknowledges each record: ACCEPT when the text went out, RELEASE when the provider timed out so someone tries again, REJECT for a bad number. A frozen member's locks run out and others get its records, and a record that fails five times is archived and, in Kafka 4.4, written to a dlq. topic. So we can run 60 instances on the 6 partitions we have, and scale back down after the sale. The price is order: records of one account can be handled at the same time by two members. Notifications don't care, but the ledger or anything that builds state per account does, and those must stay on a consumer group with partitions sized from the slowest consumer's measured rate.

deeper.html:
Batches and the last attempt. With the default share.acquire.mode=batch_optimized, the broker acquires whole record batches, so a poll can return more than max.poll.records; record_limit, used in the demos, makes the limit strict. A record on its last allowed delivery is handed out on its own; the broker logs that it "should be delivered alone in this fetch".

How many in flight. group.share.partition.max.record.locks (2000 by default) caps the in-flight records per share partition. When it's reached, members get nothing from that partition until some records finish, which is what you see when a consumer is slow and the lag stops falling.

Starting a share group from a consumer group. Kafka 4.4 (KIP-1323) can initialize a share group's start offsets from a file or from a consumer group's committed offsets, so a migration doesn't replay or skip anything. kafka-share-groups.sh --reset-offsets covers the rest.

Tiered storage in operation. Kafka 4.4 added remote.copy.lag.bytes and remote.copy.lag.ms (KIP-1241) to delay uploads, and 4.3.2 fixed a bug where size-based retention could delete data still inside retention after a leader election. Read the release notes of every patch version before you upgrade a tiered cluster.
